## Standing directives

- **DIRCP01-1** · In each Part 3, take at least one causal chain from an earlier memorandum whose later links fall in a phase this memorandum revises, and test it against the war as now written; where the new provision or free play makes it resolve differently, say so in the chain review and let it (every chain in memoranda 001–005 resolved as predicted, which is more likely tidiness than foresight)
- **DIRCP01-2** · A war-wide figure for lives saved, or any war-wide count built from a rate, must be shown at work in at least two dated events in the chapters before a later memorandum repeats it; until then it is cited as a judgment resting on its rate, with the rate named (CP01 calibration of the [X-004] lives-saved figure)
- **DIRMT01-1** · In every §4.N, state the date of the Republic's fall as its own estimate, separately from the rung: a window, the mechanisms in the cumulative force that pull it earlier and those that pull it later, and which dominate and why; "on the historical timeline" may be written only as the conclusion of that test, and a change of date is reported as a change of date and does not by itself move the rung between (a) and (b) while the ladder's overlap stands (the historical fall, twenty-five months after the last American combat troops left, satisfies the words of rung (b), and seven memoranda have kept (a) and (b) apart by the date alone)
- **DIRMT01-2** · In every §4.N, carry a running sum of the sub-band estimates that all memoranda so far have made on the same variable (American dead, ARVN battalions not lost, and the like), tagged as exercise judgments with their rates named, and say whether the sum crosses a band; and treat the American aid appropriation of 1974 and the refusal of April 1975 as events a provision can change, not as history to be carried (each memorandum judged its own saving of American lives alone, and the 1974 vote was never examined)
- **DIRMT01-3** · Where a chapter's end vector returns a variable to the historical state from a non-zero band in the phase before, the chapter must contain the dated events that produce the convergence; and in every memorandum that revises Phase VI, state in the phase's analysis the Republic's state at the end of 1974, before the last offensive, because the phase's end vector is measured after the fall and cannot record anything the fall erased (Phase V returned four countryside variables to history with no sentence on the countryside, and Phase VI's vector is blind by construction)
- **DIRMT01-4** · Where a memorandum alters an event and keeps its historical outcome, name what absorbs the difference (the enemy's choice to bypass or decline, a decision above the level the provision reached, an external fixed by law or by another government) and show it in the event; "as historically" is a conclusion, never a mechanism (in Phase VI at least six altered events in the last campaign restore the historical outcome by statement)
- **DIRMT01-5** · Where a perverse effect or a capture undoes a gain, state the net in both directions with its weight, and where several provisions' institutions fall to the same mechanism in the same years, judge them together before judging each alone (four institutions from four memoranda fall to the lapse of the American lever in 1970–71, each judged alone, and every memorandum closes on the gain undone)
- **DIRMT01-6** · The next memorandum or review whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI states the PAVN's 1972 losses in this war against the historical figure and the rebuilding time that follows, before writing 1973–75 (memorandum 005 made the measured sieges the enemy's worst battles; Phase V keeps the historical losses and Phase VI the historical rebuilding)
- **DIRMT01-7** · Every memorandum whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI tests its effects against the critical path of 1975 (the palace's orders of 13–14 March, the 1st Corps' march against the rains, and Minh's surrender) and states whether any mechanism could delay the collapse of I and II Corps by about three weeks, the threshold beyond which the assault falls into the rains; effects on fights the PAVN could bypass are reported as such (the date of the fall was carried for seven memoranda without its critical path ever being stated)
- **DIRMT01-8** · Every memorandum touching the countryside states its effect separately for the Delta, the coastal lowlands of I and II Corps, the Highlands and their peoples, and the Saigon belt, and names a place in each where the effect is shown or says why there is none (the Delta was written as a footnote, the Montagnards appear twice and FULRO never, and Binh Dinh vanished from the record after 1967)
- **DIRMT01-9** · Every provision touching the reliability of the ARVN or the territorial forces addresses the soldier's family: where it lives, what his pay buys after inflation, and what happens to it when the unit moves or the front gives way (the corps of 1975 dissolved toward their families, and no memorandum had treated them)
- **DIRMT01-10** · The enemy's decisions have authors: in each memorandum name the body or commander who took the enemy's decision of G3, and distinguish Hanoi, the B-2 Front and COSVN, and the regional fronts where they differed; treat the Soviet and Chinese supply as variables with their own politics (COSVN vanishes from the record after 1971, the Phuoc Long argument is told as one mind, and the Soviet deliveries of 1974 are absent)
- **DIRMT01-11** · Every memorandum touching the countryside or the RVNAF states its effect on rice (production, procurement and the Front's take) and on the piaster and the soldier's pay, with at least one dated event (rice appears eleven times in Phase II and once in 1972–75, the years the economy decided)
- **DIRCP02-1** · At each checkpoint, consolidate a chapter over the limit in two steps: first merge minor historical events into summary events, then merge each memorandum's own minor NEW events in that phase into one summary per memorandum, keeping every fact a later memorandum or position cites by event number; and every memorandum's §4 adds to a phase's overview and ending only one paragraph, replacing rather than appending where an earlier memorandum's paragraph states the same variable (CP02 consolidation of P1 and P2, still about 7,600 and 9,300 words over the limit after the first step)
- **DIRCP02-2** · In each Part 3 the chain taken under DIRCP01-1 must be one written by another memorandum whose terminal event this memorandum did not write; C006-4, whose terminal link no chapter carries, is the first such chain for any memorandum revising Phase V (17 of 19 chains in memoranda 006–010 resolved as their authors predicted)
- **DIRCP02-3** · Where a provision acts on a variable already at the cap of the bands in a phase, the memorandum states its increment in the running sum of DIRMT01-2 with the factors it multiplies and how they overlap, and names the target the enemy moves to in answer (POSCP02-2); a product of overlapping judgments is reported as a range with its upper bound marked (CP02 calibration of the battalions-not-broken figure)
- **DIRR01-1** · DIRCP02-3's rule for a variable "already at the cap of the bands" lapses, because the scale has no cap short of a different war: a provision that acts on such a variable re-judges its range, and the range of the facet it acts on, and the running sums of DIRMT01-2 now say which part of that range they support rather than whether they cross a band; the rest of DIRCP02-3 stands, the target the enemy moves to in answer is still named, and a product of overlapping judgments is still reported as a range with its upper bound marked (the user's change of scale, 24 Nov 2026; R01)
- **DIRR01-2** · A range marked "converted" is the old band restated, not a judgment: it is never cited as a judgment of the war, and every memorandum or checkpoint whose evidence bears on a converted entry, or on one of the four entries converted from the cap, re-judges it with a confidence and a note (R01's mechanical conversion of the end vectors)
- **DIRR01-3** · Where a variable has facets, §2 names the facet a provision acts on, and every revised phase that judges a facet names the parent's binding facet and says why it binds; the parent is never the average of its facets, and a gain on one facet is not reported as a gain on the parent unless the binding facet moved (the user's point of 24 Nov 2026 that "ARVN effectiveness" does not discriminate between urban combat, combined arms, anti-armor and the rest)
- **DIRR02-1** · A study describes the war and never changes it: no study adds, alters or cancels an event or moves the end state, and where a study finds the record inconsistent it records a question for an erratum or a checkpoint rather than settling it (the user's design of 24 Nov 2026; R02)
- **DIRR02-2** · Every memorandum whose variables a study covers is written against that study: Part 2 judges its pushes against the study's values and says plainly when the provision's effect contradicts the study and which should give way, and Part 3 records what changed in the area in the study's entry (R02)
- **DIRR02-3** · A study's value is never cited as a measurement: study values are exercise judgments on the R01 scale, an indicator a study gives carries its own provenance, and a figure the study generates carries the X-tag of its study run (X-ST01 and so on) forever (A13a; R02)

# E01 — Memorandum 003: the RQ-4B and U-2S work with GPS and satellite links, under the standing condition of 23 Nov 2026
memos: 003
location: memos/003/part1.md — the reading of "granted" in the opening paragraphs; §1.1 D1 (unit organisation) and D6 (architecture and geometry) for P003a, with every later passage that limits it to its line-of-sight tether; §1.2 D1 (configuration, unit organisation), D6 (architecture, geometry, lost link), D7 (basing), every later passage that limits it to line of sight or to the positioning array, and the card figures and negative specification for P003b
wrong: "In January 1964 there is no GPS, and there will be none for fourteen years; there are no military communications satellites in orbit [H]. … My reading, therefore, is that each RQ-4 is delivered with what it minimally needs to take off, navigate and land without satellites — a ground-based local positioning array at its home runway to stand in for differential GPS, and an inertial navigation solution corrected in flight against radar imagery of surveyed ground — and that its control and its data travel only by line-of-sight link"; card P003b: "Links: line of sight only, about 200–250 nm from a terminal" and "Navigation: inertial with radar map-matching and a local positioning array at the home runway"; negative specification: "within about 250 nm of Bien Hoa or Da Nang"; P003a D6: "A 2026 U-2 in the Middle East would also pass data beyond line of sight by satellite; in 1964 it cannot, because no satellite exists to carry it [H]", with northern collection "hours after the event, not minutes".
correct: By standing condition, the GPS and military SATCOM constellations are present from the campaign's opening [U: standing condition, set 23 Nov 2026; recorded in rules/CONFIG.toml [conditions]]. Both provisions therefore arrive and fly exactly as they fly in 2026, and the Part 1 reading is withdrawn. (1) P003b navigates by GPS-aided inertial navigation and takes off and lands on differential GPS corrections from its own Launch and Recovery Element [M003·S7]; there is no site-specific positioning array, and the "array damaged by a mortar round" failure mode does not exist. Any runway its LRE kit is set up on will serve. (2) P003b is controlled and passes its data both by line of sight and by satellite [M003·S6] [M003·S7]. Its reach is set by its endurance and the threat, not by a ground terminal: it can hold an orbit over the Red River delta, the Gulf of Tonkin, the whole of the Laotian panhandle and Cambodia, and the Mission Control Element need not sit beside the runway. A lost line-of-sight link falls back to satellite control. The Da Nang relay terminal is not needed for control; Da Nang remains a recovery alternate and a direct line-of-sight data receiver. (3) P003a passes SIGINT, radar and electro-optical data beyond line of sight by Ku-band satellite through the dorsal-pod satellite datalinks (Senior Span, Senior Spur) when out of tether range [S13], so northern collection reaches the ground station in near real time, not after landing [S14]. (4) Nothing else in Part 1 changes: the sensors, altitudes, endurance, canopy blindness, the SA-2 threat, personnel spaces and the find-and-fix limits stand as written. (5) The condition gives the constellations, not user equipment: the historical 1964–75 force has no GPS receivers or satellite terminals (A3a). Coordinates these aircraft generate are GPS-accurate; the aircraft, artillery and ground units that must use them navigate and bomb by the period's methods (map grids, LORAN, TACAN, radar bombing).
source: The user's message of 23 Nov 2026 setting the condition (not a provision; no memorandum); Part 1's own sources S6 and S7 for the RQ-4's satellite and GPS architecture; memos/003/sources.md S13 and S14 for the U-2's satellite datalinks.
consequences: No chapter carries or relies on the Part 1 reading (memorandum 003 has not reached Part 3), so no revision is needed. Memorandum 003 Part 2 is written on the corrected basis. Any later memorandum loading card 003 loads this erratum.

# Card 013 — The air campaign against the North unrestricted: an opening strike on the full target list on 2 March 1965, and MACV targeting authority with standing restrike, no Hanoi or Haiphong zones, one strike on Haiphong's port, a 15-mile Chinese buffer and no pauses

*Memorandum 013 · status part1 · full record: memos/013/ · generated by fie.py*

## P013a · Opening strike of the air campaign against the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, 2 March 1965: a planned decapitating first blow on the 2026 model of the opening nights of DESERT STORM (17 January 1991) and IRAQI FREEDOM (March 2003), against the whole of the Joint Chiefs' target list in one compressed opening, planned by MACV and CINCPAC from the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964, flown by the in-theater and carrier air forces with the B-52J, the GBU-31 and GBU-38 JDAM, the U-2S and the RQ-4B already in the record, against the command and control, air defence, airfields, power, fuel, transport and war industry of the North, with Haiphong's port infrastructure struck once and the port mined only in May 1972
one opening strike on the full target list, the JCS 94-target list of 1964 and its additions [U]; first strike on 2 March 1965 [U] · spaces none in RVN beyond the air units the record already holds; the strike is flown from Thailand, Guam, Okinawa and the carriers of TF 77 [E: basing of the 1965 air campaign] · arrives 1965-03-02 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · air

**Key figures.**
- Target list: the JCS Target Study of 94 targets, 24–27 August 1964, in five categories [M013·S1]; rejected by the White House historically [M013·S2]
- First strike 2 March 1965, planning from August 1964 [U]
- Threat on the day: about 1,500 AA guns (2,100 by another count), about 22 early-warning and 4 fire-control radars, about 36 MiG-17s, no SA-2 [M013·S5] [M013·S6] [M013·S3]
- Weight: 22–24 J sorties a day in the surge, about 440–480 GBU-31 a day [E: D5]; about 600–900 aimpoints on the list [E: D5]; the list struck in about three to four days [D]
- Kit stock on Guam, March 1965: about 8,000–12,000 GBU-31 and 15,000–25,000 GBU-38 [E: fourteen months of M005 deliveries]
- Tactical second wave: about 150–250 strike sorties on a flyable day [E: D5]
- History's benchmark: 180 aircraft lost to 24 December 1965 [M013·S6]; Hanoi and Haiphong targets from October–November 1965 [M013·S3]; Phuc Yen first struck 24 October 1967 [M013·S2]
- Within the year historically: more than 5,000 guns [M013·S6], 56 SAM sites [M013·S4]

**Negative specification.** The opening strike cannot decapitate the North. The Politburo, the Central Military Commission and the General Staff do not sit in the buildings on the list, and the Party commands the war in the South through COSVN, not through the Hanoi exchanges [E: the North's dispersed leadership]. It cannot stop the flow south: J-2 put the enemy's need from the North at 70–90 tons a day at the 1966 peak [M003], and a porter-and-bicycle Trail in 1965 does not depend on a power plant. It cannot strike Laos, where the ambassador keeps the targets, or close Haiphong, which is struck once and mined only in May 1972 [U]. It does not stop the third of the North's imports that come by rail from China [M013·S6], and the 15-mile buffer [U] leaves the last stretch of both rail lines untouched. The fighter-bombers of 1965 cannot bomb a point target at night or under the crachin of March [E: visual bombing in 1965], so on a bad week the strike is the Js' alone. It cannot prevent the Soviet SA-2 package (95 systems over the war [M013·S6]) or the Chinese support troops; it can only meet them earlier. And it does not change Washington's decision whether to bomb; it changes how much is struck once that decision is made.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the North the two and a half years of gradualism in which it built the world's densest air defence under sanctuary, from about 1,500 guns and no missiles in March 1965 to more than 5,000 guns within a year [M013·S6] and 56 SAM sites by December [M013·S4]. Phuc Yen's MiG-17s (about 36 aircraft [M013·S6]) are struck on the ground in the first hour, the four fire-control radars and about 22 warning radars [M013·S5] in the first night. It denies the North the use of its fixed infrastructure before it has learned to do without it: the power plants, the bulk fuel at Hanoi, Haiphong, Nam Dinh and Vinh, the Hanoi bridges and the rail yards, all at once and in any weather. And it denies Hanoi the reading of 1965 that the Americans would not dare: the North learns on the first night that the capital is not a sanctuary.

**Verdict.** The opening strike is the most efficient blow on the North's fixed targets that any American force in 1965 could deliver. The B-52J with about 1,400 GBU-31 in three days [D] does in the crachin of March what history's fighter-bombers did in two and a half years of weekly packages, and it catches an air defence of guns and MiG-17s before the first SA-2 arrives [M013·S3]. That buys a broken air defence for the first months of the campaign, fewer aircraft lost, and a North stripped of power, bulk fuel, bridges and airfields in a week. It does not buy the war. The North's war in the South in 1965 needs tens of tons a day [M003], carried by porters, bicycles and trucks that the list does not hold. Its leaders are not in the buildings, and its allies replace what is destroyed: Moscow ships the missiles faster and Beijing sends the engineers sooner. The strike is the end of gradualism and the start of a test the gradualists never made: whether a North that has lost everything that can be bombed will stop. History's answer, from 1972, is that it negotiates on its own timetable. The record's answer is for Parts 2 and 3.

## P013b · Standing authorities for the air campaign against the North, from 2 March 1965: COMUSMACV selects the targets north of the DMZ in place of Washington's weekly approval; standing permission to restrike any target; no restricted or prohibited zone around Hanoi or Haiphong; Haiphong's port infrastructure struck once only, everything else at and around Haiphong open; a 15-mile buffer along the Chinese border; no pauses or suspensions within the campaign; Washington keeps the decision whether to bomb at all; Laos targets stay with the ambassador; mining of the northern ports as historical, May 1972
one authority, held by COMUSMACV for the duration of the campaign [U]; buffer 15 miles [U] · spaces ~60–120 in an expanded MACV targeting and battle-damage cell at Tan Son Nhut [E: the Seventh Air Force and MACV J-2 targeting staffs of 1966–67] · arrives 1965-03-02 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Authority from 2 March 1965 [U]; COMUSMACV selects targets; standing restrike; no pauses [U]
- Buffer along China: 15 miles [U] against history's 30 miles west of 106° E and 25 east of it [M013·S2]
- Haiphong: port infrastructure struck once [U]; mined May 1972 [U]; two-thirds of the North's imports by sea, a third by rail from China [M013·S6]
- History's zones lifted: Hanoi restricted 30 miles, prohibited 10; Haiphong 10 and 4 [M013·S2]
- History's regime: 22 authorised fixed targets and 1,000 of 106,000 sorties against them in 1966 [M013·S2]; seven halts in three years and eight months [M013·S2]; Christmas halt 37 days [M013·S2]
- Targeting cell about 60–120 people at Tan Son Nhut [E: 1966–67 targeting staffs]; standing list about 200–400 targets, about 30–60 restrikes a week [E: D5]
- Soviet SA-2 deliveries over the war: 95 systems, 7,658 missiles [M013·S6]; 56 SAM sites by end 1965 historically [M013·S4]

**Negative specification.** The authority does not let me stop the bombing being stopped: the President keeps the decision whether to bomb, and the halt of 1 November 1968 stays his [U]. It does not let me close Haiphong. The port is struck once [U] and mined only in May 1972 [U], so two-thirds of the North's imports [M013·S6] keep arriving by sea, by lighter if not by crane. It does not let me strike within 15 miles of China [U], where the rail lines carry the other third [M013·S6]. It does not give me the Laos targets, which stay with the ambassador, or the Navy, whose carriers stay CINCPACFLT's and take my targets through CINCPAC. It does not make the North's fuel, stores and trucks fixed: after the first season they are dispersed under trees and in villages, as the record already shows from June 1966 (EVCP02-4). It does not measure itself honestly: the cell's battle-damage assessment is the claim of the organisation that chose the target (A13). And it does not make the North's war in the South depend on what can be bombed in the North.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the North its sanctuaries: Hanoi, the MiG bases, the SAM sites under construction, Haiphong's city and the 30-mile and 10-mile circles [M013·S2] in which history let it build, store and train. It denies the repair cycle its respite, because each repair is answered when the cell judges it done, not at the next weekly approval. It denies the pauses, the six days of May 1965 and the 37 days of Christmas 1965 [M013·S2], which the North used historically to repair, resupply and move forces south. And it denies Hanoi the reading that the war's escalation is a dial in Washington's hand that turns back whenever the President is pressed.

**Verdict.** The authority is the change the theater asked for throughout the war, and it buys what was asked for. A campaign against the North's fixed targets is fought as a campaign: targets chosen in the theater, struck when ready, restruck when repaired, without sanctuary and without pause. With the opening strike it makes the North's air defence a lesser and later threat, saves aircraft and crews, and keeps the bridges, power and rail of the North down for as long as Washington allows. It does not buy the end of the North's war in the South. Haiphong's cargo keeps coming by lighter after the port's one strike, and the Chinese rail keeps coming through the buffer. The Trail runs on porters, trucks and fords that the record has already shown no bombing stops. The halt that ends the campaign stays the President's, and removing the pauses spends his tolerance faster. The theater gets the campaign it wanted. The record will show whether that campaign was ever the war's decisive instrument, and history's 1972 suggests it was decisive only for the terms, not for the outcome.

## P005a · Boeing B-52J Stratofortress, programme-of-record configuration: B-52H airframe re-engined with eight Rolls-Royce F130 turbofans (Commercial Engine Replacement Program), Raytheon AN/APQ-188 AESA radar (Radar Modernization Program), digital cockpit displays, 1760 Internal Weapons Bay Upgrade, GPS-aided navigation and the H's electronic-warfare suite, replacing every B-52 one for one
Every B-52 in the USAF inventory replaced one for one [U]: about 600 airframes in 1964 across SAC [E: 744 B-52s built, less attrition and retirements of early B and C models], of which the force committed to Southeast Asia follows the historical deployment: 30 in mid-1965 [H], about 50–70 through 1966–67 [E: sortie rates of about 800 a month by mid-1967 per S9], about 90–100 from early 1968 [E: 1,800 sorties a month from February 1968 per S9], 210 at the 1972 peak [M005·S9] · spaces 0 in RVN for the bomber force itself [E: Arc Light flew from Guam, U-Tapao and Okinawa]; about 40 in RVN for an enlarged Arc Light liaison and target-coordinate cell at MACV and Seventh Air Force [E: the historical ARC LIGHT liaison element plus a coordinate-mensuration team]; outside RVN, maintenance manpower about 10–20% below the historical B-52 force [E: F130 needs no off-wing overhaul per S4, five-man crew per S2 against the D's six] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, INTERDICT, FIX, SUSTAIN · air

**Key figures.**
- Programme status: CERP Milestone B 1 June 2026; AN/APQ-188 Milestone C 21 August 2026; IOC mid-FY2033 [M005·S1] [M005·S3]
- Crew: 5 (no tail gunner) against the B-52D's 6 [M005·S2] [H]
- Payload: about 70,000 lb mixed ordnance [M005·S2]
- JDAM load: 20 (8 internal, 12 external) [M005·S6]; GBU-38 about 30–40 [E: D3]; unguided Mk 82 about 51 [E: D3] against the Big Belly's 108 [M005·S9]
- Speed 650 mph (Mach 0.86); ceiling 50,000 ft [M005·S2]
- Range: H 8,800 miles unrefuelled [M005·S2]; J estimated 10,500–12,000 miles [E: F130 about 30% more fuel-efficient, S4]
- Guam–South Vietnam round trip unrefuelled with full conventional load [E: D5 range estimate]
- Maintenance manpower about 10–20% below the historical B-52 force; no F130 off-wing overhaul [E: D2 and S4] [M005·S4]
- Estimated loss rate over Hanoi a third to a half of the historical Linebacker II rate of 15 in 729 sorties [E: D7] [H]
- In-theater strength follows history: 30 in 1965, 210 at the 1972 peak [H] [M005·S9]

**Negative specification.** The B-52J finds nothing under canopy: its AN/APQ-188 radar and targeting pod see bridges, ferries, roads and open ground, not regiments under triple canopy, and it addresses neither half of the find-and-fix problem (A6). It is not a better carpet-bomber: it carries about 51 unguided 500 lb bombs [E: the B-52H conventional load in D3] against the Big Belly B-52D's 108 [M005·S9], so an Arc Light box flown by Js with unguided bombs is half as dense. Its precision lives entirely in its GPS weapons and in the coordinates fed to them; no 1965 ground unit can pass it a digital coordinate or read a grid reference finer than about 100 m [E: 1:50,000 map reading to six figures]. It does not escape the SA-2 over Hanoi, whose engagement range of about 25 miles [E: published SA-2 engagement envelope] exceeds the JDAM's 15-mile glide [M005·S7]. It is not in service in 2026: its performance figures are the B-52H's plus programme claims [M005·S1] [M005·S3]. It does not transfer to the VNAF. It does not lift any political constraint: where it may bomb is still decided in Washington.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the protection of weather and of distance from base, since GPS weapons fall through the monsoon and the bomber reaches any target unrefuelled from Guam. Against fixed targets, it denies the enemy safety in point defences, since GPS weapons can be released up to 15 miles outside them [M005·S7]. It denies him the habit of reading Arc Light's intentions from the tanker rendezvous [E: the tanker rendezvous was visible to the trawler off Guam, S9].

**Verdict.** The B-52J is a better aircraft than the B-52D in almost every respect that can be measured: it burns about 30% less fuel [M005·S4], flies to the South from Guam without tankers [E: D5 range estimate], risks five men instead of six [M005·S2], and carries twenty 2,000 lb GPS weapons [M005·S6] where the D carried none. But the war Arc Light fought was a war of area bombing on targets located by intelligence hours or days old, and for that war the J is a worse carpet and an equal guess. Its real value is the GBU-31 and GBU-38 it carries, and their value depends on coordinates: on the U-2S and the Global Hawks of Memorandum 003, and on what the ground war can locate. Where Washington lets it strike fixed targets in the panhandle and the North, the J is a transformation of what one bomber can destroy in one night in any weather. In the South, against an enemy under canopy who chooses when to fight, it is a more efficient way to do what the D did.

## P005b · GBU-31 Joint Direct Attack Munition, 2,000 lb class: GBU-31(V)1/B on the Mk 84 general-purpose bomb and GBU-31(V)3/B on the BLU-109 penetrator, Boeing GPS-aided INS tail kit, with FMU-152 or equivalent programmable fuze, 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 8,000–12,000 kits a year from 1964 for the bomber force [E: about a third of a JDAM production line of 25,000–40,000 kits a year, the rest going to the GBU-38 and to stocks] · spaces ~60 in RVN [E: a coordinate-mensuration and weaponeering cell at MACV J-2 and Seventh Air Force working in shifts]; kit build-up and loading crews of about 150–250 at Andersen and U-Tapao outside RVN [E: munitions maintenance squadron increments] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · air

**Key figures.**
- Weights: GBU-31(V)1/B (Mk 84) 2,036 lb [M005·S7], GBU-31(V)3/B (BLU-109) 2,115 lb [M005·S7]
- CEP 5 m or less with GPS; 30 m or less for 100 s without GPS; 9.6 m in operational test [M005·S7]
- Range up to 15 miles; release up to 45,000+ ft [M005·S7]
- B-52J load: 20 (8 internal, 12 external) [M005·S6]
- Mk 84 fill about 945 lb [E: published Mk 84 fill]; BLU-109 penetrates about 1.8–2.4 m reinforced concrete [E: D3]
- Supply to theater about 8,000–12,000 kits a year [E: D1], enough for about 400–600 full sorties a year [D]
- Coordinate cell about 60 men at MACV J-2 and Seventh Air Force [E: D2]; 1:50,000 map coordinates in the mountains 100–300 m off [E: D2]
- Kit cost about $22,000 (FY2007) [M005·S7]

**Negative specification.** The GBU-31 has no seeker and finds nothing: it goes to a coordinate and cannot follow anything that moves. Its accuracy of 5 m or less [M005·S7] is relative to the coordinate given, and in 1965 the best coordinate available is a map grid with errors of 100–300 m in the mountains [E: D2], unless the U-2S and Global Hawk imagery of Memorandum 003 is measured to produce it [M003]. It cannot equip Arc Light: about 8,000–12,000 kits a year [E: D1] support about 400–600 full sorties a year [D] against up to 1,800 Arc Light sorties a month [M005·S9]. The BLU-109 penetrates about 1.8–2.4 m of reinforced concrete [E: D3] and does not reach the deep levels of tunnel systems 3–10 m down in laterite [E: D3]. It cannot be released by any VNAF aircraft, none of which has a 1760 interface. It changes no political constraint: the bridges of the North can be struck only where Washington allows.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the protection of weather over his fixed targets, and the safety of point defences around them. It also denies him the safety of numbers: a bridge that survived hundreds of unguided bombs now falls to a handful. Fixed infrastructure with a known coordinate becomes untenable, which pushes the enemy towards infrastructure he can move, hide or rebuild overnight.

**Verdict.** The GBU-31 makes every fixed target with a measured coordinate a target that dies in one strike, in any weather, from 1965. That changes the air war against bridges, ferries, depots, power plants and fortified positions as completely as the laser-guided bomb changed it in 1972, and seven years earlier. It does not change the war against an enemy whose valuable things are not fixed: men, trucks under trees, rice in caches and regiments in the forest. Its value in the South is limited by the coordinate, and in the North by Washington. Its supply limits it to a precision force inside Arc Light, not a replacement for it.

## P005c · GBU-38 Joint Direct Attack Munition, 500 lb class: Boeing GPS-aided INS tail kit on the Mk 82 or BLU-111 bomb body, with FMU-152 or equivalent programmable fuze, 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 15,000–25,000 kits a year from 1964 [E: the larger share of a JDAM production line of 25,000–40,000 kits a year] · spaces ~0 additional in RVN [E: shares the P005b coordinate cell]; about 100 loaders and kit builders outside RVN [E: the 500 lb kit's higher count per sortie] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, FIX · air

**Key figures.**
- Weight 558 lb (Air Force) or 590 lb (Navy) on Mk 82/BLU-111; length 92.6 in [M005·S7] [M005·S8]
- CEP 5 m or less with GPS; range up to 15 miles; release up to 45,000 ft [M005·S7]
- B-52J load about 30–40 [E: §1.1 D3]
- Mk 82 fill about 190 lb [E: published Mk 82 fill]
- Danger-close for a 500 lb bomb about 400 m in the open [E: danger-close tables]; historical Arc Light safety distance 3 km, later about 1 km [E: Arc Light safety distances at Khe Sanh and An Loc]
- Supply to theater about 15,000–25,000 kits a year [E: D1]; about 400–800 full sorties a year [D]
- Guided sorties of both sizes about 800–1,400 a year against Arc Light's 800–1,800 a month [D] [M005·S9]
- 1965 ground coordinate by map about 100 m accuracy [E: 1:50,000 map reading]

**Negative specification.** The GBU-38 has no seeker and cannot follow a moving target; the Laser JDAM that can is not supplied [M005·S8]. Its CEP of 5 m or less [M005·S7] applies to the coordinate it is given, and the 1965 infantryman, controller or forward observer can give a coordinate only to about 100 m by map [E: 1:50,000 map reading], because no historical ground unit has a GPS receiver (CONFIG conditions). It is not an artillery substitute for the minute-to-minute fight: it comes when a B-52J is overhead and cannot be adjusted. It does not defeat the enemy's hugging tactics; it narrows the gap he must close. Danger-close for a 500 lb bomb remains about 400 m in the open [E: danger-close tables for 500 lb bombs]. A wrong coordinate near a perimeter is a precise fratricide. Supply supports about 400–800 full sorties a year [D]. It cannot be released by any VNAF aircraft.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the time and safety to dig siege works within a kilometre of a besieged base: positions he holds long enough to be measured can be struck one by one, at night and in cloud, a few hundred metres from the defenders. It narrows the safety margin his hugging tactics depend on, and it denies him safety for trucks, guns and parks in the open whose positions are known.

**Verdict.** The GBU-38 gives the B-52 something it never had: the ability to put 30–40 separate 500 lb bombs on 30–40 known positions near friendly troops, in any weather [E: §1.1 D3 carriage]. In the sieges of this war, at Plei Me, Con Thien, Dak To, Khe Sanh, Kontum and An Loc, where the enemy closed on a fixed position and dug in long enough to be measured, that is a large change in what the bombers can do for the men inside the wire. Elsewhere it is limited by the 1965 infantryman's map, by the enemy's choice to fight where he cannot be measured, and by supply.

## P005d · Quickstrike family of aircraft-laid bottom influence mines: Mk 62 (500 lb), Mk 63 (1,000 lb) and Mk 64 (2,000 lb) on Mk 80-series bomb bodies, Mk 65 (2,000 lb class thin-walled case), and Mk 64 Mod 5 Quickstrike-ER with the JDAM-ER wing kit, with Mk 57 and Mk 71 target detecting devices (magnetic, seismic, pressure and acoustic), 2026 configuration
Supplied with the B-52J force at realistic production rates [U]: about 3,000–6,000 mines a year from 1964, of which a few hundred Quickstrike-ER [E: conversion kits on existing bomb bodies, with target detecting devices the rate limit; QS-ER still in demonstration per S15] · spaces ~0 in RVN [E: assembly and preset at Guam and U-Tapao]; about 40–60 Navy mine assembly and preset specialists outside RVN [E: a Mobile Mine Assembly Group detachment] · arrives 1964-01-01 · INTERDICT, STRIKE · naval

**Key figures.**
- Family: Mk 62 (500 lb), Mk 63 (1,000 lb), Mk 64 (2,000 lb) bomb-body mines, Mk 65 (2,390 lb, depths to 600 ft), in service 1983 [M005·S11] [M005·S13]
- Quickstrike-ER: Mk 64 with GBU-64v1 JDAM-ER kit, released more than 40 miles out; 12 per B-52H pending certification [M005·S15]
- Standard laying below about 500 ft at about 300 knots or less [M005·S14]; B-52 from about 1,000 ft at 500–600 km/h [M005·S16]
- Detecting devices: Mk 57 and Mk 71 (magnetic, pressure, seismic, acoustic; ship classification) [M005·S12] [M005·S16]
- B-52J loads: about 51 Mk 62 [E: §1.1 D3]; about 20 Mk 64 or Mk 65 [E: §1.1 D3]
- Supply about 3,000–6,000 mines a year, a few hundred ER [E: D1]
- Haiphong mining prohibited until May 1972; 27 ships stayed in Haiphong after the May 1972 mining [H] [M005·S17]
- Fill: Mk 62 about 190 lb, Mk 63 about 445 lb, Mk 64 about 945 lb [E: published Mk 80-series fills]

**Negative specification.** Quickstrike does not detect wooden sampans, bamboo rafts or floating drums: its magnetic setting ignores them, and pressure or seismic settings may catch only the larger wooden junks [E: pressure signatures of larger hulls]. It does not close the Trail: it closes waterways, and the historical Destructor fields of 1965–68 in the panhandle did not stop the flow [M005·S17]. It cannot be laid in Haiphong or the northern ports before May 1972, nor in Cambodian waters, under the modelled constraints [H]. Standard Quickstrikes are laid at 500–1,000 ft [M005·S14] [M005·S16], which over defended crossings means AAA; safe laying needs the Quickstrike-J or the Quickstrike-ER, which is still in demonstration in 2026 [M005·S15]. Its fields need reseeding every few weeks [E: D10] and cannot be switched off after laying. Its value against land vehicles is not established in my sources.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the use of steel-hulled craft on mined waterways and coastal approaches south of the 20th parallel, and the use of Haiphong from May 1972, without sweeping or loss. It forces him onto wooden craft, roads and trucks. It denies him safe passage at the ferries and fords where boats and barges must cross.

**Verdict.** Quickstrike is a better Destructor and a better Mk 52. Its greatest use in this war, the closing of Haiphong, is prohibited until May 1972 by Washington, and when it comes the historical mines did the job. In the panhandle's rivers and coastal lighterage it raises the toll on the North's waterborne logistics from 1965 and forces the load onto wooden craft and trucks, but it does not reduce what arrives in the South by much, because the Trail has the road. It is a modest provision on its own and a valuable one only if Washington lets it be used against the ports.

# Card 003 — Two U-2S Dragon Lady and four RQ-4B Global Hawk Block 40 high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft

*Memorandum 003 · status complete · full record: memos/003/ · generated by fie.py*

## P003a · Lockheed Martin U-2S Dragon Lady (Block 20), 2026 configuration: ASARS-2A synthetic aperture radar with moving-target indication, SYERS-2C multispectral electro-optical and infrared camera, ASIP signals intelligence payload, with a deployable ground exploitation station
2 aircraft [U] · spaces ~220 [E: four to five pilots and a mobile-crew cell, about 90 maintainers and life-support technicians, about 20 contractor field engineers, and an exploitation and SIGINT cell of about 100 in shifts] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIND, STRIKE, INTERDICT · isr

**Key figures.**
- Quantity: 2 U-2S Block 20 [U], about one in fourteen of the 2026 fleet of 27 U-2S [M003·S1]
- Ceiling above 70,000 ft; speed about 410 mph; range 7,000+ miles [M003·S1]; F118-GE-101 of 17,000 lb [M003·S1]
- Mission about 9 hours normally, 12+ possible; no air refuelling [M003·S5]
- Sensors: ASARS-2A radar (search, spotlight, moving targets, all weather), SYERS-2C EO/IR, ASIP SIGINT [M003·S1] [M003·S9]
- Datalink: real time within about 220 miles of a ground station, stored beyond [M003·S5]; ground stations at Bien Hoa and Da Nang [E: geometry]
- Sortie rate: about one a day, about 25 a month [E: two aircraft, five pilots]
- Coverage: on the order of 100,000 sq nm of radar search per sortie [E: swath of 60–100 nm over about 3,000 nm of track]
- Personnel: about 220 [E: pilots, maintainers, contractors, exploitation cell]
- Cost: about US$30,000–40,000 per flying hour [E: comparable high-altitude ISR]
- Threats: immune to guns and MiG-17s; vulnerable to the SA-2 from April 1965 [H]

**Negative specification.** The U-2S cannot see under the canopy, with radar or camera, and the enemy's base camps, hospitals, depots and regiments are under the canopy. It cannot see the VC infrastructure in the hamlets at all; it addresses the main-force half of find-and-fix only. It does not provide real-time coverage beyond about 220 miles of a ground station; northern collection arrives after landing. Two aircraft give about one sortie a day, not persistent surveillance: it looks at a place, then goes away. Its SIGINT locates transmitters to kilometres, not metres, and only while the enemy transmits. Its camera is useless in monsoon cloud. It has no weapons, and its product is worth only what a strike, raid or airmobile force can do with it inside the hours the location stays true. Over the North it is not invulnerable once SA-2s arrive in 1965, and a loss cannot be replaced. Its products cannot safely be shared with ARVN except in sanitised form, because the Joint General Staff is penetrated.

**Denies the enemy.** The cover of weather and darkness over open ground: roads, rivers, fords, truck parks, depots and construction in the North, Laos and the base areas can no longer be hidden by cloud or night. Radio security at regiment and above: every transmission becomes a possible location. The surprise of a newly built road, airfield, SAM site or base area, which radar change detection reveals within days.

**Verdict.** A large improvement in what MACV and the air campaign know about the enemy's rear — the Trail, the North's transport system, the base areas and the radio nets of his higher headquarters — at a modest cost in people and none in lives. It is the best strategic reconnaissance in the world in 1964 by a wide margin, and over the North it will make target selection and damage assessment honest and air losses lower. It does not find a regiment in the jungle tonight, it does not find the VCI, and two aircraft cannot watch anything continuously. Its value to the war in the South is as a cue — for the direction-finding aircraft, the long-range patrols, the Special Forces and the bombers — and its value depends on there being something fast enough to act on what it finds. Real, durable, and not decisive alone.

## P003b · Northrop Grumman RQ-4B Global Hawk Block 40, 2026 configuration: MP-RTIP active electronically scanned array radar with simultaneous ground moving-target indication and synthetic aperture imaging, with a Launch and Recovery Element and a Mission Control Element
4 aircraft [U] · spaces ~380 [E: six to seven three-person mission crews for one continuous orbit, an LRE detachment, about 140 maintainers and contractor technicians, and a GMTI and radar-imagery exploitation cell of about 150 in shifts] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIND, INTERDICT, STRIKE · isr

**Key figures.**
- Quantity: 4 RQ-4B Block 40 [U], almost half the 2026 USAF fleet of 9 [M003·S2]
- Sensor: MP-RTIP AESA radar, simultaneous GMTI and SAR, maritime modes [M003·S6] [M003·S7]; no camera, no SIGINT [M003·S2]
- Ceiling 60,000 ft; speed about 357 mph; endurance 32+ hours, 24 hours on station at 1,200 miles [M003·S2]
- Orbit: one continuous 24-hour orbit sustained, a second for about a third of the time [E: four aircraft at about 75% availability]
- Coverage: roughly 20,000–40,000 sq km watched for moving targets per orbit; vehicles and boats tracked to about 100–150 nm [E: wide-area GMTI]
- Links: line of sight only, about 200–250 nm from a terminal [E: by analogy with the U-2's on-tether figure in S5]; terminals at Bien Hoa and Da Nang
- Navigation: inertial with radar map-matching and a local positioning array at the home runway [E: a reading of "granted"; the 2026 RQ-4 uses GPS and differential GPS, per S7]
- Personnel: about 380 [E: crews, LRE, maintainers, exploitation]
- Cost: about US$18,900 per flight hour (2013) [M003·S7]; about US$130 million per aircraft (2013) [M003·S7]
- Threats: immune to guns and MiGs; highly vulnerable to the SA-2 from mid-1965 [E: judgment from the system's design and the theater's conditions]

**Negative specification.** The RQ-4B Block 40 carries a radar and nothing else: no camera, no infrared, no SIGINT. It cannot see under canopy, so it does not see the main force in its base areas or most of the Trail. It cannot reliably see men on foot moving slowly or in small groups. It cannot tell a VC sampan from a farmer's, or a supply truck from a civilian lorry; its tracks are movement, not identity, and firing on them under the historical rules will kill civilians. It has no satellite links in 1964: control and data are limited to about 250 nm of a ground terminal [E: line-of-sight geometry], and Hanoi and Haiphong are out of reach. It depends on a reading of "granted" for navigation and landing without GPS, and on a single ground segment at Bien Hoa. It is vulnerable to the SA-2 and, unlike the U-2, has no pilot to avoid one. Four aircraft sustain one continuous orbit, not two. It does not touch the VCI. It does not reduce tonnage arriving in the South; it shows where tonnage moves in the open, and only a strike reduces it.

**Denies the enemy.** The cover of night and weather for anything that moves in the open: trucks on roads, sampans on canals and rivers, trawlers at sea, and columns crossing open ground. It forces the enemy to move under canopy or in small groups by day and in rain, which slows him and costs him. It denies the seaborne infiltration route its anonymity among coastal traffic.

**Verdict.** A persistent, all-weather, day-and-night watch on everything that moves in the open within about 250 nm of Bien Hoa or Da Nang [E: line-of-sight geometry] — the sea approaches, the Delta's waterways, the roads of the Laotian panhandle and the North's southern provinces. Its strongest use is at sea, where a steel-hulled trawler is a large, slow, isolated target among junks, and the coast is otherwise unwatched; its second is the Trail's open stretches once the enemy has trucks on it from 1965. Under canopy it is blind, against the infrastructure useless, and in the Delta and the populated coastal plain it is dangerous, because it shows movement without identity. It does not find the main force where the main force lives. It shows where it moves, which is less, and it is worth what can be put on a track inside the hour.

**Pushes:** INFIL.sea -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], FIND.main_force +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], STRIKE.responsiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], POP.civilian_harm +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.personnel_demand +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], AIR.north_effect +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** FIX.capability, LOG.helicopter_hours, TRAIL.capacity, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia, INFIL.sea, LOG.distribution, AIR.north_defences, INTL.chinese_intervention_risk, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control

# Card 011 — American Political Tolerance Package: the Watergate break-in never happens, a quarter of the historical draftees serve as volunteers, and the My Lai massacre does not happen

*Memorandum 011 · status complete · full record: memos/011/ · generated by fie.py*

## P011a · No Watergate: the Committee for the Re-election of the President's break-ins at the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate building, 28 May and 17 June 1972, never happen, and with them the arrests, the cover-up, the Senate Watergate Committee, the special prosecutor, the impeachment proceedings and the resignation; Richard Nixon serves his second term to 20 January 1977
Both break-ins removed [U]; everything that followed from them removed with them; the abuses before May 1972 (the 1969 wiretaps, the 1971 'plumbers') stay in the war but are never exposed by a Watergate investigation [E: D1 reading] · spaces 0 [U] · arrives 1972-05-28 · SUSTAIN · other

**Key figures.**
- Break-ins removed: 28 May and 17 June 1972 [M011·S10]; Nixon serves to 20 Jan 1977 [D]
- Case–Church: House 325–86 (26 Jun 1973), Senate 73–16 (29 Jun 1973), signed 1 Jul, cut-off 15 Aug 1973 [M011·S6]; chance it survives in substantially historical form 60–75% [X-011]
- War Powers override (7 Nov 1973, 18 days after the Saturday Night Massacre): about even odds without Watergate [X-011]
- 1974 midterm: history +49 House, +5 Senate for the Democrats [M011·S4]; without Watergate about +15–30 House [X-011]
- FY1975 RVNAF military aid: history about $700 million against about $1.1 billion in FY1974 [H]; with the provision about $850 million – $1.1 billion [X-011]
- Nixon's approval 24% in early Aug 1974; 57% said his conduct warranted removal [M011·S11]
- Nixon to Thieu, 14 Nov 1972: the United States "will react very strongly and rapidly to any violation" [M011·S5]
- Ford's request of 10 Apr 1975: $722 million military, $250 million economic and humanitarian [M011·S9]
- Gallup "mistake": about 60% in 1971 and in 1973 [M011·S1]

**Negative specification.** - It does not make the war popular. Gallup's "mistake" share was about 60% in 1971 and in 1973, before Watergate's worst months [M011·S1]; the provision acts on the President's authority and the size of the 1974 midterm swing, not on opinion of the war.
- It probably does not repeal Case–Church. The amendment passed 325–86 and 73–16 in June 1973 [M011·S6], veto-proof margins reached before the Saturday Night Massacre of 20 October 1973 [M011·S10]; I judge a 60–75% chance the 15 August 1973 cut-off survives in substantially its historical form [X-011].
- It does not restore American combat power. The B-52s, fighter-bombers and gunships of 1972 are withdrawn on the historical timetable; the provision changes whether a President could send them back, not whether they are there.
- It changes nothing before May 1973: the 1972 election, the Easter Offensive, Linebacker and Linebacker II and the Paris Agreement run as history ran them.
- It reaches the battlefield only through money and Hanoi's reading of American will; it touches no hamlet, no regiment and no road.
- It may make Saigon complacent: a Thieu who still believes the President's letters is less likely to plan a defence without the bombers.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies Hanoi the evidence of American paralysis in 1973–74: a President fighting impeachment, then resigning, and a successor without a mandate facing a Congress elected in the scandal's wake. It does not deny the North the Case–Church prohibition, which Hanoi can read in the statute book whoever is President.

**Verdict.** This is a real provision, and it is smaller than its name. Removing Watergate keeps a re-elected President in office with his authority intact through the two years when the Republic was left to fight alone. On my best judgment, that is worth a fiscal 1975 military appropriation of perhaps $850 million – $1.1 billion instead of $700 million, a midterm swing of 15–30 House seats instead of 49, and an enforcement threat Hanoi has to take more seriously in 1974 [X-011]. It is probably not worth the repeal of Case–Church, which Congress passed by margins Watergate did not create, and it does not change the American public's settled view that the war was a mistake. Its largest effect is on the North's calendar, which in 1975 tested whether America would answer the fall of a province. Whether a strong Nixon would have answered it against the law is the question that decides what this provision is worth. I cannot answer it from the record, and I will not pretend to.

**Pushes:** US.political_tolerance.administration +4..+7 (medium), US.political_tolerance.congress +2..+4 (low), US.political_tolerance.public +0..+1 (medium), NEGOT.position +1..+3 (low), GVN.political_stability +0..+2 (low), VNAF.capability.maintenance +1..+3 (low), ARVN.self_sufficiency.logistics +0..+2 (low) · **Depends on:** US.political_tolerance, ARVN.self_sufficiency, HANOI.will, US.credibility_gap

## P011b · Volunteers in place of a quarter of the draft: of the men historically inducted by the Selective Service System from 1964 to the end of inductions in 1973, one in four enlists voluntarily instead; the same men serve, in the same services, specialties, terms and tours; Selective Service draft calls are a quarter smaller in every month
One quarter of historical inductions [U]: about 464,000 of the 1,857,304 men inducted Aug 1964 – Feb 1973 [D]; draft calls a quarter smaller in each year, from about 84,000 instead of 112,386 in 1964 to about 287,000 instead of 382,010 at the 1966 peak and about 37,000 instead of 49,514 in 1972 [D] · spaces 0 [U] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical inductions Aug 1964 – Feb 1973: 1,857,304 [M011·S2]; a quarter, about 464,000, now volunteers [D]
- Peak year 1966: 382,010 historical inductions, about 287,000 under the provision [D]
- Draftees who served in RVN Jan 1965 – May 1973: about 648,500 [M011·S12]; about 162,000 now volunteers [D]
- Draftees were about 30% of the war's dead and about half of Army enlisted dead [M011·S3]; under the provision about one in thirteen of all the dead changes from draftee to volunteer [D]
- Draft offences: about 210,000 accused, 8,750 convicted, 3,250 jailed, 30,000–100,000 abroad [M011·S7]; with the provision perhaps 10–20% fewer accused [X-011]
- Gallup "not a mistake": 60% about six months into the commitment, 48% Jul 1967, 44% Oct 1967 [M011·S1]
- Personnel spaces: 0; force size unchanged [U]

**Negative specification.** - It does not make the force larger or the war cheaper in men: the same men serve, in the same jobs, on the same terms and tours [U]. If the volunteers had signed three-year Regular Army enlistments instead of serving two years as draftees, the Army would have needed fewer men and the draft calls would have fallen by more than a quarter; the ruling does not take that reading, and I do not.
- It does not reduce casualties: about 30% of the war's dead were draftees [M011·S3]; under the provision a quarter of them, about one in thirteen of all the dead, die as volunteers instead [D], and the number of the dead is unchanged.
- It does not touch the deferments, which spared more than half of the 27 million eligible [M011·S7], or the class and race of who was drafted.
- It does not end draft resistance: the men who would have resisted are disproportionately among those still drafted; I judge resistance falls by perhaps 10–20%, not 25% [X-011].
- It does not reach the Marine Corps, Navy or Air Force, whose enlisted men were already volunteers [M011·S3], or the RVNAF.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies Hanoi a quarter of the most visible face of the American antiwar movement: the induction notices, the draft trials and the young men in Canada. It denies the Front nothing in the South.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision with a real effect. A quarter fewer induction notices, about 464,000 fewer over the war [D], takes some heat out of the war's sharpest domestic grievance in every year from 1965 to 1972. It improves the morale of Army rifle companies at the margin, most of all in the bad years of 1969–71, and it changes the status of about one in thirteen of the dead [D]. It does not change the number of the dead, the deferments that made the draft unjust, or the casualty lists and the absence of victory that turned the country against the war. I judge it a small gain in the public's tolerance and a small gain in unit quality [X-011]. That gain would buy a few months of patience at the margins, not a different war at home. If the turn of opinion was driven more by the draft than I think, it buys more. If it was driven by the dead, as I think it largely was, it buys less.

**Pushes:** US.political_tolerance.public +1..+3 (medium), US.political_tolerance.congress +0..+2 (low), US.unit_quality +1..+3 (medium) · **Depends on:** US.casualties, US.personnel_demand

## P011c · No My Lai: the killing of the villagers of Son My village (My Lai 4 and My Khe), Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province, by Company C, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry and Company B, 4th Battalion, 3rd Infantry, 11th Infantry Brigade, Americal Division, on 16 March 1968 does not happen; isolated and stipulated, with no cause inside the war; other atrocities stay historical
One event removed [U]: the 347–504 villagers killed historically [H] live; the cover-up, the Ridenhour letters, the Hersh report, the Peers inquiry and the Calley court-martial do not occur [D] · spaces 0 [U] · arrives 1968-03-16 · SECURE, SUSTAIN · other

**Key figures.**
- Date and place removed: 16 Mar 1968, Son My village (My Lai 4 and My Khe), Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province [H]
- Units: Company C, 1/20th Infantry and Company B, 4/3rd Infantry, 11th Infantry Brigade, Americal Division, under Task Force Barker [H]
- Lives saved: 347 (US Army figure) to 504 (Vietnamese figure) [H]
- Removed with it: the cover-up, Ridenhour's letters (Mar 1969), Hersh's report (13 Nov 1969), the Peers inquiry, Calley's conviction (29 Mar 1971) [H]
- Calley verdict polling, Apr 1971: 11% approved; 70% said scapegoat; 79% said the life sentence too harsh [M011·S8]
- Gallup "mistake": 53% Aug 1968; 55% average 1969–70 [M011·S1]
- Ruling: isolated and stipulated; no cause inside the war; every other atrocity stays historical [U]

**Negative specification.** - It saves the 347–504 villagers of Son My [H]; it does not change the conditions that produced the massacre. By ruling it is isolated and stipulated [U]: the Americal Division, the 11th Brigade, Task Force Barker, the body-count command climate and every other atrocity of the war stay as history recorded them.
- It does not make the war popular: Gallup's "mistake" share was already 53% in August 1968 and averaged 55% in 1969–70 [M011·S1], before My Lai was known in November 1969.
- It does not remove a turn in mass opinion: in April 1971 only 11% approved the Calley verdict, 70% thought him a scapegoat, and 79% thought the life sentence too harsh [M011·S8].
- It removes the Peers inquiry and the Army's reckoning with the command climate and reporting chain that produced and concealed the massacre; that cost is real.
- It does not touch the countryside beyond one village: Quang Ngai remains a Front province, and Son My remains a Front village.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies Hanoi and the Front the war's most powerful single piece of propaganda, at home and abroad, and the antiwar movement its emblem. It denies the enemy nothing in the field.

**Verdict.** Between 347 and 504 people live, and that is reason enough to be glad of this provision [H]. Measured as an act of war policy, it is small. My Lai did not turn the American public against the war, which had turned before the massacre was known [M011·S1], and when the public did react, in 1971, it sided with the lieutenant [M011·S8]. What My Lai did was give the war's opponents their emblem and the credibility gap its starkest proof. Removing it narrows that gap noticeably and adds a little to the public's tolerance [X-011]. It also removes the Peers inquiry and the reckoning that followed. Because the provision is isolated by ruling, the command climate that produced the massacre runs on unexamined. That is the provision's most important effect on the war, and it points the wrong way.

# Card 001 — Accelerated land-to-the-tiller reform and an enforced GVN anti-corruption programme

*Memorandum 001 · status complete · full record: memos/001/ · generated by fie.py*

## P001a · Land-to-the-Tiller Programme, 1964 (accelerated and enhanced): zero retention of tenanted rice land, free distribution to the present tiller, confirmation of Viet Minh and Viet Cong distributions, US-financed landlord compensation, and a fit-for-purpose aerial-photo titling apparatus
One national programme: about 1.0–1.2 million ha of tenanted land to about 850,000–950,000 families [E: Prosterman's 1960–61 tenancy census and the GAO's 1970 LTTT target of 1 million ha to 800,000 tenants] · spaces ~260 US personnel, of whom ~60 military spaces [E: USAID land and survey advisers in each province plus an Army engineer topographic detachment; the 1970s LTTT advisory staff was 31] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, SUBVERT · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Terms: zero retention of tenanted rice land; owner-cultivators keep up to 15 ha; worship land 5 ha; recipients up to 3 ha (Delta) and 1 ha (Centre); land free; 15-year transfer ban [M001·S2]
- Compensation 2.5 × annual paddy yield, 20% cash and 80% eight-year bonds at 10% [M001·S2], indexed to paddy price in this provision [U]; about $200–280 million at 1964 prices, about 77% US-financed [E: 1970 average of about $282/ha [M001·S3] scaled to 1964]
- Target about 1.0–1.2 million ha to about 850,000–950,000 families [E: Prosterman's census and the GAO's 1970 target]
- Delta 1960–61: 1,175,000 farm families, about 855,000 farming tenanted land; average rent 34% of crop, Centre about 50% [M001·S2]
- Apparatus rate about 40,000–60,000 ha a month if all villages were accessible [E: 120 teams at two villages a team-month]; 1970 programme averaged about 28,000 ha a month [D] (1,007,217 ha in 36 months [M001·S3])
- 1964 titles limited by security to about 15,000–30,000 ha a month, about 150,000–300,000 ha by end-1964 [E: villages accessible by day]
- Rice lands photographed in about three months by two aircraft at 25 cm [D] (from the UltraCam Eagle Mark 3 frame [M001·S10]); no satellite navigation in 1964, so ground control by optical survey [H]
- About 9,000 Vietnamese staff and 260 Americans, of whom about 60 are military spaces [E: organisation in D1–D2]
- Historical comparison: Land to the Tiller (1970) titled 1,198,000 ha with 953,000 titles by end-1973, nearly 40% of cultivated land [M001·S4]

**Negative specification.** It does not make a single hamlet secure at night, and it cannot be delivered in a hamlet the government does not hold: there it is a promise and a registered claim, not a title. It does not stop Viet Cong conscription or coercive taxation, which do not depend on persuasion. It does not reach the main force or Hanoi's will. It does not produce gratitude on any schedule; its effect accrues over seasons and years in what the rural population believes the government's return means. It does not touch the highlands, the plantations or the cities. It is not a guarantee against reversal by the next junta, and it injures the landed families from which much of the officer corps comes. The claim that the 1970 programme cut Viet Cong recruitment by 80% [M001·S11] is the designers' own organisation's claim and is not adopted here. 2026 survey practice that depends on satellite navigation or data networks does not work in 1964; the photography is tied to ground control by optical survey [H].

**Denies the enemy.** The land argument: the claim that the government's return to a hamlet means the landlord's return, and with it the logic that a family must send its sons to the revolution because only the revolution's victory keeps the land [M001·S5]. Where titles are delivered and defended, it denies the infrastructure the consent it taxes by; where they cannot be delivered, it denies the enemy the certainty that the peasant has nothing to gain from the government's arrival.

**Verdict.** This is the provision the theater needs assessment said could touch its first-ranked deficit, and it does: it changes, at a stroke and on paper, the answer to the question that defines the Republic in the countryside, which is what the government's arrival means to a tenant. Six years earlier than history, with the 1970 law's terms and the repairs that law needed, it is a potentially war-shaping political instrument at a negligible cost in money and men. It is not a security measure and it cannot outrun security: in 1964 the government can deliver titles in perhaps a fifth to a half of the Delta's hamlets, and a title in a hamlet the enemy holds at night is a list of targets. Its value therefore depends on what holds the hamlets, on whether the juntas keep it and keep their troops from escorting landlords back, and on whether the officials executing it are honest. Its great virtue is that once a million families have received land, no later government or enemy can easily take that fact back. Its impact on 1964 is modest; its impact on the war, if it survives, is large and slow, and I will say so at full weight.

## P001b · GVN Anti-Corruption Programme with Enforcement Mechanism: an independent Commission Against Corruption on the Hong Kong ICAC model with powers of arrest, search, seizure and compelled asset declaration, a special anti-corruption court, an independent RVNAF pay-and-muster verification service, and a joint US–GVN Aid Compliance Board empowered to suspend aid to a command or ministry
One national commission of about 2,000 Vietnamese staff with about 320 US advisers, investigators and auditors [E: ICAC's 1,213 staff for a city of about 7 million, scaled for a country of about 15 million and an armed force of about 514,000] · spaces ~320 US personnel, of whom ~140 military spaces [E: Army CID agents, finance and audit officers and muster teams; the rest USAID, Treasury and GAO-trained civilians] · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, SUSTAIN, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Design: independent Commission on the Hong Kong ICAC model (Operations, Corruption Prevention, Community Relations; powers to arrest, search and seize) [M001·S12], a Special Court, a Pay and Muster Verification Service, a joint US–GVN Aid Compliance Board able to suspend aid to a command, importer or province, asset declarations for majors and above, and a limited amnesty for pre-1964 petty corruption [U]
- About 2,000 Vietnamese staff and about 320 Americans, about 140 of them military spaces [E: ICAC's 1,213 staff [M001·S12] scaled for the RVN]
- Musters about 480 units a month, the whole RVNAF of about 514,000 [M001·S24] about twice a year; biometric enrolment complete in about nine months [E: 60 teams and 600 kits]
- About 1,500–2,500 cases opened and 300–500 brought to court a year; the court tries about 300–400 [E: a new commission's caseload]
- Ghost-soldier benchmarks: Iraq 50,000 (2014) [M001·S16]; Afghanistan about 42,000 fewer on biometric validation (2019) [M001·S15]; Afghan pay system with 7,714 records absent from the biometric database [M001·S14]
- If 5–10% of RVNAF rolls are ghosts, about 25,000–50,000 paper spaces exposed [E: no reliable count exists; phantom troops reported in the press in 1965 [M001·S17]]
- The lever: Commercial Import Program obligations of $397 million in 1966 [M001·S21], whose counterpart piasters paid the army, police and civil service [M001·S20]

**Negative specification.** It does not end corruption in the Republic, and it does not reach the junta itself without a patron stronger than the generals it would accuse. It does not make officers competent; it removes some who are corrupt and exposed, and only where a replacement exists. Biometric identity cards do not stop a commander who controls who is enrolled; only the independent, physical muster does that, and only where a team can reach. It does not pay a soldier enough to live on in an inflating economy, so petty corruption born of need survives it. It is not an instrument against the Viet Cong. It is likely to be used by factions against each other. Its enforcement lever, the Aid Compliance Board, is American and cannot be transferred; it weakens as American aid falls, and every suspension costs the Republic part of its claim to be its own government (POSTNA-6).

**Denies the enemy.** One of the Front's strongest themes, a corrupt regime that robs its own soldiers and people, where convictions are visible and reach above the district. Some of the black market through which American goods reach the enemy, and some of the bribes by which his agents buy documents and posts. Above all it denies him the hollow battalion: a unit carried at a strength it does not have, whose commander and whose advisers do not know how weak it is until it breaks.

**Verdict.** This is a smaller provision than it sounds and a more important one than its figures will show. It will not clean the Saigon government, and in a junta that makes coups its most likely failure is to become one faction's weapon against another. What it can do reliably is the physical part: count the army, put the pay in the soldier's hand, and end the ghost battalion, which strengthens the RVNAF's real fighting power, reduces one cause of desertion, and gives this headquarters a true strength return for the first time (G-10). What it may do, if it is protected and the American lever is used and seen to be used, is change what an officer expects to happen to him if he buys a command or sells his men's rice, which reaches the officer corps (G-4) where nothing in an arsenal can. Its greatest value may be to the land programme (P001a), whose officials it watches. Its greatest cost is political: it threatens the incomes of the men who make governments, and it gives the Americans a hand on the Republic's throat that the enemy will name for what it is.

**Pushes:** GVN.corruption -2 [old band ≈ -7..-5], GVN.political_stability -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], ARVN.leadership +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.desertion -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], GVN.admin_capacity +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], POP.gvn_legitimacy +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.credibility_gap -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], ADVISE.leverage +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], INTEL.penetration -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], US.political_tolerance +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** LOG.helicopter_hours, GVN.political_stability, ADVISE.leverage, US.political_tolerance, GVN.police, INTEL.penetration, ARVN.leadership

# Card 004 (short: key figures and negative specifications omitted; full card in build/cards/) — Modern infantry small arms for US, ARVN and RF/PF: M4A1 URG-I with Aimpoint CompM5, M110A2 squad marksman rifle, M249 squad automatic weapon

*Memorandum 004 · status complete · full record: memos/004/ · generated by fie.py*

## P004a · M4A1 carbine with the Upper Receiver Group – Improved (URG-I: Geissele Automatics upper, Daniel Defense 14.5-inch 1:7 barrel, mid-length gas, Mk16 13.5-inch M-LOK rail, SureFire SF4P flash hider) and Aimpoint CompM5 2 MOA red-dot sight, firing M855A1 5.56mm, 2026 configuration
All rifles and carbines of US forces and the RVNAF, and all RF/PF [U]: a first increment of about 600,000 carbines and sights in 1964, rising to about 1.7–1.9 million cumulative by 1972 [E: RVNAF 514,000 in 1964 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72 per S9, US strength rising to about 540,000 at peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~250 [E: about 120 new-equipment training spaces in the first year, about 80 small-arms and optics repair technicians at the depots, and about 50 added small-arms advisers to the RF/PF training centres; no troop ceiling is set, but each space still costs] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, FIX, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · ground

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the main force and the local force the firepower advantage that the AK-47 gave them over the ARVN, the Regional Forces and the Popular Forces from 1964 until those forces received the M16 in 1968–69. It denies the Front's propaganda the outgunned government soldier, and it denies the attacking company the outpost whose garrison has eight-round Garands and carbines.

**Verdict.** This is a real improvement, concentrated where the war is decided: at night, at the wall of an outpost, in the first seconds of a contact. For the American forces it is an improvement and no more, because the M16A1 they historically carry is the same calibre and its 1967 crisis was fixable. For the ARVN infantry it closes, four years early, the firepower gap that history recorded and that ARVN soldiers felt. For the Regional and Popular Forces, who historically fought five years with carbines against AK-47s, it is the largest change: the territorials are the men who hold the hamlets at night, and an outpost that is not outgunned holds longer. What it does not do is just as plain. It does not find anyone, does not make an absent platoon present, does not touch the VCI, and every outpost lost arms the enemy with it. It improves the force inside its rung; I do not expect it to move the rung by itself.

**Pushes:** ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], RFPF.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.unit_quality +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.casualties -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2], POP.night_control +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], VC.local_force +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], US.political_tolerance +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** LOG.distribution, LOG.ports, ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.leadership, GVN.corruption, ENEMY.engagement_control, FIND.main_force, RFPF.effectiveness, ARVN.desertion, ARVN.self_sufficiency, SUBVERT.defection, VC.main_force, US.casualties

## P004b · Knight's Armament Company M110A2 7.62mm semi-automatic rifle (20-inch free-floated match barrel, integral suppressor, 12-inch M-LOK handguard, collapsible stock) with SIG Sauer TANGO6T 1-6x24mm first-focal-plane illuminated variable-power scope, firing M118LR and M80A1 7.62mm, issued one per infantry squad as the designated marksman's rifle, 2026 configuration
One per US and ARVN infantry squad [U]: about 5,000 rifles and scopes in 1964, about 13,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: about 120 ARVN, Ranger, Airborne and Marine battalions of about 36 squads in 1964 rising to about 180 by 1972, plus up to about 112 US Army and Marine manoeuvre battalions at the 1968–69 peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~120 [E: marksman instructor teams of about 60 at the training centres and about 60 match-rifle and scope armourers; the marksmen themselves are squad members already counted] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, STRIKE · ground

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy free movement at 300–800 m in the open [E: the marksman's practical range], where his snipers, machine gunners and leaders have historically been out of reach of the M16 and the AK alike. It denies his own snipers the uncontested ground around a firebase or an outpost, and it costs his sapper teams forming for an assault under flare light.

**Verdict.** This is a narrow tool and, in its terrain, a good one. In the Delta, the coastal plain, the paddy country and around the firebases, a trained marksman in each squad kills the enemy's leaders and gunners at ranges nobody else in the squad can reach, and the suppressor keeps him alive to do it again. Under the canopy, where much of the main-force war is fought, it does nothing a carbine does not. It depends on training the ARVN does not yet have, on squad leaders who know how to use it, and on the marksman staying alive. Its effect on the war is real and small: it improves the squad's fire where the fight is in the open, and it does not change which side chooses the fight.

**Pushes:** FIX.capability +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, LOG.distribution, FIND.main_force

## P004c · FN America M249 5.56mm light machine gun (PIP-standard, 465mm barrel, collapsible stock) with SIG Sauer TANGO6T 1-6x24mm scope (DWLR-556 reticle), firing linked M855A1 from 200-round pouches or STANAG magazines, at squad level in US and ARVN infantry in place of the BAR and the squad's automatic weapon, 2026 configuration
At squad level in US and ARVN infantry [U]: about 5,200 guns in 1964, about 17,000–19,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: one per ARVN squad in place of its BAR, two per Army squad and three per Marine squad in place of the fire teams' automatic rifles, on the battalion counts of P004b, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~100 [E: machine-gun instructor teams of about 40 and about 60 armourers for barrels, gas systems and feed trays; the gunners are squad members already counted] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE · ground

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy's RPD-armed squads the advantage of a belt-fed gun against an ARVN squad with a 20-round BAR, and it denies the enemy assault the pause when the BAR reloads.

**Verdict.** This is the most combat-significant of the three provisions at squad level. A belt-fed gun at the centre of each ARVN squad gives it a base of fire it has never had: it can hold an enemy in contact, cover a withdrawal, break an assault on a perimeter. In a meeting engagement or an ambush, the squad that has a belt-fed gun and uses it well wins more often. It is heavy, it eats ammunition, it jams if it is not cleaned, and its gunner is the enemy's first target. It does not find the enemy or decide when the fight happens. It makes the squads that fight better at fighting, which matters every day in this war, though it is not where the war's hardest problem lies.

**Pushes:** FIX.capability +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], ARVN.effectiveness +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4], LOG.distribution -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] · **Depends on:** LOG.distribution, ENEMY.engagement_control, ADVISE.leverage, PAVN.strength_south
